kzz7yh-a02616-d1e293.summary: Opens the division of the text (divisio textus) of Lombard's work: the whole of the Sentences divides into a prologue ('Cupientes'), the treatise proper ('Veteris ac novae legis'), and a kind of recapitulation at the end of Book IV ('Hic de pedibus sedentis').
claims: The Sentences divides into prologue, treatise, and final recapitulation.

kzz7yh-a02616-d1e316.summary: Divides Lombard's prologue into three parts aimed at making the hearer attentive, docile, and benevolent, and justifies this order by Boethius (De disciplina scholarium): the disciple's subjection consists in attention, benevolence, and docility, i.e. attentive to hear, docile to understand, benevolent to retain.
claims: Lombard's prologue aims to render the reader attentive, docile, and benevolent.
This tripartite aim follows the Boethian account of the disciple's dispositions.

kzz7yh-a02616-d1e340.summary: Subdivides the 'attentive' part according to three things that make the hearer attentive: the arduousness of the matter ('Cupientes'), the teacher's diligence ('Desiderium hortatur proficiendi'), and the malice of opponents ('Quamvis non ambigamus').
claims: Attention is secured by the difficulty of the matter, the teacher's diligence, and the opponents' malice.

kzz7yh-a02616-d1e358.summary: Divides the passage on arduousness into the difficulty of undertaking the work and Lombard's confidence of completing it ('Consummationis fiduciam').

kzz7yh-a02616-d1e365.summary: Divides the passage on the teacher's diligence into two motives: zeal for the Church and the insistence of the brothers' requests ('Non valentes studiosorum fratrum').
claims: Lombard's diligence is motivated by zeal for the Church and fraternal petition.

kzz7yh-a02616-d1e381.summary: Completes the division of Lombard's prologue: the opponents' malice concerns both attacking truth and teaching falsehood ('Quorum professio'); the 'docile' part ('Horum igitur') appeals to the evident utility and certain truth of the doctrine ('Ex testimoniis veritatis'); the 'benevolent' part ('Non igitur debet') appeals to the goodness of the work against charges of superfluity and to the author's humility against obstinacy of private judgment ('In hoc autem tractatu').
claims: Docility is produced by the doctrine's evident utility and certain truth.
Benevolence is produced by the work's goodness and the author's humility.

kzz7yh-a02616.summary: The Praeambulum to the Prologue gives Richard's divisio textus of Lombard's prologue ('Cupientes'). After dividing the whole Sentences into prologue, treatise, and final recapitulation, Richard reads the prologue as a rhetorical exordium that, following Boethius, makes the reader attentive (by the arduousness of the matter, the author's diligence, and the malice of opponents), docile (by the doctrine's evident utility and certain truth), and benevolent (by the work's goodness and the author's humility). The item maps the structure of Lombard's text rather than arguing a thesis.
claims: Lombard's prologue is structured to render the reader attentive, docile, and benevolent.
The Sentences comprises prologue, treatise, and recapitulation.
